title: Latham & Watkins Legal Engineering Attorney and Legal Workflow Engineer Roles
author: Latham & Watkins

dup.label: latham watkins legal engineering attorney legal workflow engineer roles

sib.t: The emergence of the 'legal engineer' role (job postings and commentary, 2025-2026)

dom.t: Legal engineering: Implementation extends beyond prompting

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source describes document-services workflow coordination and workplace-experience roles, but provides no substantive position on AI capability, legal engineering, verification, task-specific evaluation or service redesign. It therefore does not establish support for or opposition to the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The EntityClusterSummary contains no title, description, key points or quotations, so there is insufficient evidence to assess the source’s position relative to the cluster synthesis.

st.t: Legal engineering: Implementation extends beyond prompting
st.an: Latham & Watkins’ role specifications directly support the proposition that legal engineering is a dedicated, cross-functional function extending beyond prompting to workflow redesign, expertise codification, governance, quality measurement and continuing adoption. The materials prescribe intended staffing and operating practices rather than reporting achieved productivity or accuracy gains.
qs: Contributes to training and adoption strategies for AI-powered transactional tools, helping ensure  attorneys and staff understand best practices for effective AI utilization in their work.

kp.k: Dedicated engineering roles support practice-group AI workflows
kp.d: The Legal Workflow Engineer job description, last updated February 26, 2026, specifies an individual-contributor role within AI & Legal Innovation, reporting to a legal engineering manager. Its responsibilities encompass workflow design, prompt engineering, quality assurance and continuous improvement in collaboration with attorneys, technology colleagues and knowledge teams. These are prescribed job responsibilities, not reported implementation results.
qs: The Legal Workflow Engineer is a key individual contributor within the AI & Legal Innovation team,  responsible for designing, developing, and optimizing AI-powered workflows that support a legal practice  group.

The Legal Workflow Engineer focuses on prompt engineering, workflow development, quality assurance,  and continuous improvement of AI outputs to ensure accuracy, consistency, and alignment with attorney  expectations.

kp.k: Legal engineering converts expertise into executable systems
kp.d: The Legal Engineering Attorney posting assigns responsibility for translating legal expertise into prompts, schemas, evaluation suites, playbooks and end-to-end workflows. It explicitly covers decomposition of both transactional and litigation work into measurable tasks with defined decision points and quality criteria suitable for AI execution.
qs: This role will be responsible for designing the AI‑native systems that translate elite legal expertise into reliable, repeatable, machine‑executable outputs, including prompts, schemas, evaluation suites, playbooks, and end‑to‑end workflows, while decomposing complex transactional and litigation workflows into discrete, measurable tasks with defined inputs, outputs, decision points, and quality criteria suitable for AI execution.

kp.k: AI-first redesign includes review gates and exception handling
kp.d: The attorney role is tasked with redesigning manual workflows for AI-first execution while determining work allocation, review gates and exception handling. The posting therefore specifies controlled workflow design rather than claiming that legal work can proceed without review; it does not identify which tasks must receive human verification.
qs: Re‑engineering existing manual workflows for AI‑first execution, determining the appropriate allocation of work, placement of review gates, and handling of exceptions

kp.k: Senior practitioners’ tacit knowledge becomes structured reusable material
kp.d: The attorney role includes codifying senior practitioners’ negotiation and drafting knowledge in machine-readable form, translating practice materials into executable rules, and curating precedents for prompting, fine-tuning and evaluation. This describes the intended conversion of practice knowledge into reusable AI-system inputs.
qs: Codifying the tacit knowledge of senior practitioners, including fallback positions, market terms, negotiation flexibility, and drafting conventions, in machine‑readable form

Translating practice group playbooks, checklists, negotiation positions, and house style into structured artifacts, including prompts, schemas, decision trees, and rule sets that production AI systems can execute against
Curating exemplar matters, precedents, and work product into reference packs that drive few‑shot prompting, fine‑tuning, and evaluation

kp.k: Quality evaluation becomes an explicit specialist capability
kp.d: Both roles require systematic attention to output quality. The workflow engineer monitors KPIs, quality metrics and attorney satisfaction, while the attorney posting seeks experience with evaluation rubrics, golden datasets, comparisons and error taxonomies. These are evaluation responsibilities and qualifications; the materials provide no measured accuracy or productivity results.
qs: Monitors and reports on KPIs, quality metrics, and attorney satisfaction measures for AI-powered  workflows, using data-driven insights to guide optimization and iteration.

Exhibit practical experience designing evaluation rubrics and conducting structured quality measurement of AI outputs, including the use of golden datasets, head‑to‑head comparisons, and error taxonomies

kp.k: Workflow engineering combines transactional knowledge and technical skills
kp.d: The workflow engineer specification seeks knowledge of M&A, finance and capital markets alongside prompt and knowledge engineering, governance, and familiarity with retrieval-augmented generation, context windows and fine-tuning. It requires a bachelor’s degree or equivalent and at least three years of relevant experience, without stating a J.D. requirement.
qs: Solid understanding of transactional legal practice, including M&A, finance, and capital markets  workflows, with the ability to translate practice requirements into AI workflow specifications.
Technical aptitude with AI systems and familiarity with concepts such as retrieval-augmented  generation, context window management, and fine-tuning approaches.

Minimum of three years’ experience in in legal technology, knowledge management, or legal  practice, with demonstrated experience in AI systems, prompt engineering, or workflow  optimization required.
Bachelor’s degree or equivalent required, preferably in Law, Computer Science, Information  Systems, or a related field.

kp.k: Attorney engineering requires legal practice and operationalization experience
kp.d: The Legal Engineering Attorney posting requires a J.D., at least three years of substantive legal practice with ownership of complex transactional or advisory matters, and at least two years of full-time experience operationalizing expertise in an engineering or comparable innovation role. It also seeks structured-data proficiency and preferably experience at legal AI companies, law-firm innovation teams, ALSPs or software companies building lawyer tools.
qs: A J.D. from an accredited law school
A minimum of three (3) years of substantive legal practice experience at a law firm or in‑house legal department, with ownership of complex transactional or advisory matters

A minimum of two (2) years of full‑time experience as a Legal Engineer, Legal Knowledge Engineer, Legal Workflow Engineer, Innovation Attorney, or comparable role focused on operationalizing legal expertise into AI-driven systems and workflows

Demonstrate working proficiency reading and writing structured data formats, including JSON, JSON Schema, YAML, and Markdown, with the ability to understand schemas, enumerations, and conditional logic independently
Experience at a legal AI company, law firm innovation team, alternative legal services provider, or software company building tools for lawyers, preferably

kp.k: AI deployment includes governance, pilots and long-term planning
kp.d: The workflow engineer contributes to multi-year roadmaps aligned with firm strategy and practice priorities, applies governance to development and deployment, and supports pilots with defined success criteria and deployment recommendations. The source describes an intended development process, not evidence that particular pilots succeeded.
qs: Executes on the strategic vision for AI-enabled workflows, contributing to multi-year roadmaps for  AI optimization initiatives aligned with firm strategy, practice group priorities, and attorney needs.
Supports pilot programs and proof-of-concept initiatives for new AI workflows and optimization  techniques, contributing to evaluation, success criteria definition, and deployment  recommendations.
Ability to apply governance frameworks that support disciplined development, testing, and  deployment of AI workflows for transactional practice.

kp.k: Training and vendor collaboration accompany workflow development
kp.d: The workflow engineer is expected to help attorneys and staff adopt transactional AI tools and collaborate with platform vendors and internal technology teams on performance feedback and product enhancements. Adoption support and external product collaboration are explicit parts of the role, alongside technical development.
qs: Contributes to training and adoption strategies for AI-powered transactional tools, helping ensure  attorneys and staff understand best practices for effective AI utilization in their work.

Collaborates with AI platform vendors and internal technology teams to provide feedback on  system performance, identify enhancement opportunities, and support product development to  better serve transactional workflows.

kp.k: Confidentiality remains an explicit engineering attorney responsibility
kp.d: The attorney posting expressly assigns protection and maintenance of sensitive, confidential and privileged information. This is a stated role obligation; the document does not detail particular security controls or professional-rule interpretations.
qs: Protecting and maintaining any highly sensitive, confidential, privileged, financial, and/or proprietary information that Latham & Watkins retains

kp.k: Engineering attorney compensation and office options are specified
kp.d: The Legal Engineering Attorney listing states an annual pay range of USD $220,000.00–$250,000.00 and potential placement in New York, Boston, Chicago, Washington, D.C., or Los Angeles, with possible hybrid working. These are advertised employment terms, not observed compensation outcomes.
qs: This role will be located in either our New York, Boston, Chicago, Washington, D.C., or Los Angeles offices.
Please note that this role may be eligible for a flexible working schedule that allows for a hybrid and in-office presence.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Latham & Watkins describes an intended shift from manual legal workflows to AI-first execution, with legal expertise translated into structured, machine-executable systems.
pts.d: The Legal Engineering Attorney posting presents this as an assigned responsibility rather than a measured finding or a market-wide forecast. Complex transactional and litigation workflows are to be decomposed into tasks with specified inputs, outputs, decision points, and quality criteria. Practice playbooks and senior practitioners' tacit knowledge are to become prompts, schemas, decision trees, rule sets, and reference materials. The intended change includes allocating work between AI execution and review gates and handling exceptions; it is not a claim of wholly autonomous legal service delivery.

pts.k: Latham assigns dedicated engineering work to making legal AI outputs consistent, practice-specific, and subject to continuous quality improvement.
pts.d: The Legal Workflow Engineer role combines prompt engineering, workflow development, knowledge engineering, quality assurance, performance monitoring, and adoption support. The source describes a sustained operational function rather than simply giving lawyers access to a general-purpose tool. The Legal Engineering Attorney also designs structured evaluation using reference datasets and error classifications. These are planned quality-control and evaluation activities, not reported benchmark results or evidence that every output is verified before reliance.

pts.k: The careers materials specify distinct legal-AI occupations combining substantive legal knowledge with technical implementation skills.
pts.d: Latham specifies a J.D.-qualified Legal Engineering Attorney role alongside a Legal Workflow Engineer role whose stated requirements do not include a J.D. The attorney position requires substantive practice experience and experience operationalizing legal expertise into AI systems; the workflow position accepts backgrounds in legal technology, knowledge management, or legal practice. This documents the firm's intended staffing capabilities, not net employment growth, associate replacement, or a changed partner-to-associate ratio. Additional firm listings describe technical AI delivery and client-facing AI innovation leadership.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is employer-authored role specifications and recruitment materials, not measured legal-service outcomes.
pts.d: The detailed responsibilities, qualifications, reporting arrangements, and advertised compensation provide documentary evidence of the capabilities Latham seeks to organize and recruit. The Legal Engineering Attorney posting advertises annual pay of $220,000–$250,000. The document offers no completed pilot results, productivity estimates, accuracy scores, cost savings, client outcomes, or displacement data. References to KPIs, evaluation suites, and pilots specify work to be undertaken, not results already achieved. A careers-page capture says the requested job could not be found, so that portion does not establish that the requested vacancy remained open; nor do the materials establish that the positions were filled.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source describes 2026 staffing intentions and ongoing, multi-year AI development, conditional on practice needs, quality controls, and disciplined deployment.
pts.d: The Legal Workflow Engineer description was last updated February 26, 2026; the supplied capture note is dated September 4, 2026. Responsibilities include multi-year roadmaps and continuing optimization, without a completion deadline or quantified forecast. Deployment is to be governed by technical feasibility, legal-practice standards, testing, pilot evaluation, and attorney needs. The attorney role also explicitly requires protection of confidential and privileged information.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate affected groups are Latham's practice lawyers, senior knowledge holders, legal engineers, technology and knowledge teams, and staff adopting AI workflows.
pts.d: The Workflow Engineer description emphasizes transactional practices, specifically M&A, finance, and capital markets; the Legal Engineering Attorney description extends to litigation workflows. Attorneys supply practice requirements and expertise and receive tools and training; senior practitioners' knowledge is codified; engineers build and evaluate systems; technology, knowledge management, and vendors coordinate development and deployment. The attorney vacancy lists New York, Boston, Chicago, Washington, D.C., and Los Angeles as possible locations. A separate client-services leadership listing extends the intended organizational change to client-facing AI engagement, but no concrete client savings or public access-to-justice effects are claimed.
